running.headline: Train with run programs
running.body: Follow a Zone 2 Base plan with heart rate guidance, set a weekly distance goal and race countdown, take a guided fitness test to set your paces, and review splits after every run.

routes.headline: Plan and follow routes
routes.body: Draw routes on a satellite map, snap them to roads, generate loops of a set distance, and follow a saved route on your Apple Watch.

checkIn.headline: Check in in one flow
checkIn.body: Log your mood, measurements, and a progress photo in three quick steps. Find Daily Check-In in the + menu.

strength.headline: Smarter strength workouts
strength.body: Pin the set to do now, swap exercises in a tap, keep your sets when you replace an exercise, and load the bar with the plate calculator.

heartRate.headline: Heart rate zones, your way
heartRate.body: Set your own max and resting heart rate and zone method, then dig into detailed heart rate reports.

reports.headline: See how your habits connect
reports.body: Browse nutrition, hydration, sleep, mood, and measurement reports, then use Compare to see whether one habit goes with another, or whether something changed since you started a new habit.

watch.headline: Your day on your wrist
watch.body: The watch app now comes to Apple Watch and Wear OS. See your goals, log water, weight, fasting, and medications, and run workouts that save to your diary, with effort ratings, jump rope, and route following on Apple Watch. Choose your pages in Watch settings.

weeklyGoal.headline: Set a weekly weight goal
weeklyGoal.body: Choose how much weight you want to lose or gain each week and Sparky works out your daily calorie target.

medications.headline: Track your medications
medications.body: Add your medications, set dose schedules, log each dose from the dashboard with optional reminders, and review adherence with a calendar and dose log.

cycle.headline: Track your cycle & pregnancy
cycle.body: Comprehensive tracking for cycle phases, symptoms, flow, and pregnancy progress with tailored insights and goal adjustments.

workout.headline: Revamped workout workflows
workout.body: Streamlined exercise logging, updated exercise library management, and improved multi-set performance tracking.

ios.headline: A Liquid Glass look
ios.body: Turn on Liquid Glass navigation for translucent tabs and headers that pick up the color behind them. Toggle it anytime in App settings.

chat.headline: Chat with your AI coach
chat.body: Ask Sparky to log meals, plan what to eat, and answer questions about your day through chat.

widget.headline: Calories on your home screen
widget.body: See where your day stands at a glance. Add SparkyFitness from your home screen's widget gallery.

photo.headline: Snap a meal, log the macros
photo.body: Estimate nutrition from a photo when you're short on time.

w4.baby: The embryo has implanted and the placenta is beginning to form.
w4.mom: You may have just missed your period. Early hormones are rising.

w5.baby: The neural tube — the start of the brain and spinal cord — is forming.
w5.mom: Early symptoms like tender breasts and fatigue may begin.

w6.baby: A tiny heart begins to beat and pump blood.
w6.mom: Morning sickness can start around now.

w7.baby: Arm and leg buds are appearing; the brain is growing fast.
w7.mom: Your uterus is starting to expand, though it is not visible yet.

w8.baby: Fingers and toes are forming and tiny movements begin.
w8.mom: Blood volume is increasing to support your baby.

w9.baby: Essential organs are formed; the baby is now officially a fetus.
w9.mom: You might notice mood changes from shifting hormones.

w10.baby: Vital organs are working and tiny nails start to develop.
w10.mom: Your waistline may start to change.

w11.baby: The baby can open and close its fists; bones are hardening.
w11.mom: Nausea often begins to ease in the coming weeks.

w12.baby: Reflexes are developing; the baby may curl its fingers and toes.
w12.mom: End of the first trimester is near — energy often returns.

w13.baby: Tiny fingerprints are forming and vocal cords are developing.
w13.mom: Welcome to the second trimester — often the most comfortable.

w14.baby: The baby can make facial expressions and may suck its thumb.
w14.mom: You may start to feel more like yourself again.

w15.baby: The baby can sense light and is moving amniotic fluid.
w15.mom: You might notice a little baby bump appearing.

w16.baby: The baby can hear sounds and its heart pumps a lot of blood daily.
w16.mom: Some people feel the first flutters ("quickening") around now.

w17.baby: Fat stores begin to form and the skeleton hardens.
w17.mom: Your center of gravity is shifting as your bump grows.

w18.baby: The baby can hear your voice and may respond to sounds.
w18.mom: You may feel more defined movements now.

w19.baby: A protective coating (vernix) covers the skin.
w19.mom: Round-ligament aches are common as things stretch.

w20.baby: Halfway there! The baby is swallowing and developing taste buds.
w20.mom: Your anatomy-scan ultrasound often happens around now.

w21.baby: The baby is moving more, with regular sleep and wake cycles.
w21.mom: You may feel kicks more strongly and regularly.

w22.baby: Lips, eyelids and eyebrows are more distinct.
w22.mom: Your bump is now clearly visible.

w23.baby: The baby can hear loud sounds and is putting on weight.
w23.mom: Swelling in feet and ankles can begin.

w24.baby: The lungs are developing; the baby reaches a viability milestone.
w24.mom: You may have a glucose screening test soon.

w25.baby: The baby is growing hair and its startle reflex is developing.
w25.mom: Backaches are common as your bump grows.

w26.baby: The eyes begin to open and lungs practice breathing motions.
w26.mom: You might feel rhythmic movements — the baby has hiccups.

w27.baby: Brain activity increases sharply; the baby may recognize your voice.

w28.baby: The baby can blink and its eyelashes have formed.
w28.mom: Prenatal visits often become more frequent now.

w29.baby: Muscles and lungs continue maturing; bones are fully formed.
w29.mom: You may feel short of breath as your uterus rises.

w30.baby: The baby can regulate its own temperature better now.
w30.mom: Fatigue can return in the third trimester.

w31.baby: The baby is putting on weight quickly and moving often.
w31.mom: You may notice Braxton-Hicks practice contractions.

w32.baby: The lungs are practicing breathing; the baby often settles head-down.
w32.mom: Consider starting your birth plan and hospital bag.

w33.baby: The baby's bones are hardening, though the skull stays soft.
w33.mom: You may feel more pressure in your pelvis.

w34.baby: The central nervous system and lungs are maturing well.
w34.mom: Fatigue and swelling are common; rest when you can.

w35.baby: The baby is filling out; most systems are nearly ready.
w35.mom: Your provider may check the baby's position.

w36.baby: The baby is likely head-down and gaining ~28 g a day.
w36.mom: Weekly checkups usually begin around now.

w37.baby: The baby is considered early term and practicing breathing.
w37.mom: Watch for signs of labor and keep your bag ready.

w38.baby: Organs are ready for life outside; the baby has a firm grasp.
w38.mom: You may feel the baby "drop" lower into your pelvis.

w39.baby: The baby is full term and ready to meet you.
w39.mom: Any day now — watch for regular contractions.

w40.baby: Your due date is here! Babies arrive on their own schedule.
w40.mom: If labor hasn't started, your provider will discuss next steps.

cooked_salmon.name: Cooked salmon
cooked_salmon.note: Well-cooked, low-mercury fish is a great source of omega-3s. Aim for 2–3 servings/week.

tuna_canned_light.name: Tuna (canned light)
tuna_canned_light.note: Limit to ~2 servings/week; choose light over albacore for lower mercury.

swordfish.name: Swordfish
swordfish.note: High-mercury fish should be avoided during pregnancy.

sushi_raw.name: Sushi (raw)
sushi_raw.note: Raw fish carries a risk of parasites and bacteria. Cooked rolls are fine.

shrimp_cooked.name: Shrimp (cooked)
shrimp_cooked.note: Fully cooked shellfish is low-mercury and safe.

soft_cheese_unpasteurized.name: Soft cheese (unpasteurized)
soft_cheese_unpasteurized.note: Unpasteurized soft cheeses risk listeria. Pasteurized versions are fine.

hard_cheese.name: Hard cheese
hard_cheese.note: Hard and pasteurized cheeses are safe.

pasteurized_milk.name: Pasteurized milk
pasteurized_milk.note: Pasteurized dairy is safe and a good calcium source.

deli_meat_cold.name: Deli meat (cold)
deli_meat_cold.note: Heat until steaming to reduce listeria risk.

undercooked_meat.name: Undercooked meat
undercooked_meat.note: Cook meat thoroughly to avoid toxoplasmosis and bacteria.

cooked_chicken.name: Cooked chicken
cooked_chicken.note: Fully cooked poultry is a safe protein source.

runny_raw_eggs.name: Runny/raw eggs
runny_raw_eggs.note: Cook until firm, or use pasteurized eggs, to avoid salmonella.

coffee.name: Coffee
coffee.note: Limit caffeine to about 200 mg/day (roughly one 12 oz coffee).

alcohol.name: Alcohol
alcohol.note: No amount of alcohol is considered safe during pregnancy.

herbal_tea.name: Herbal tea
herbal_tea.note: Some herbs are not recommended; check specific teas with your provider.

cooked_leafy_greens.name: Cooked leafy greens
cooked_leafy_greens.note: Wash well; a great source of folate and iron.

unwashed_produce.name: Unwashed produce
unwashed_produce.note: Wash thoroughly; avoid raw sprouts, which can harbor bacteria.

liver_pate.name: Liver / pâté
liver_pate.note: Very high in vitamin A, which can be harmful in large amounts.

peanuts.name: Peanuts
peanuts.note: Safe unless you have a personal allergy; a good protein source.

honey.name: Honey
honey.note: Safe for you in pregnancy (avoid giving to infants under 1 year).

acetaminophen.name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
acetaminophen.note: Generally considered first-line for pain/fever at recommended doses. Confirm with your provider.

ibuprofen.name: Ibuprofen (Advil)
ibuprofen.note: Avoid especially in the third trimester; use only if your provider advises.

aspirin.name: Aspirin
aspirin.note: Only low-dose if prescribed; regular-dose aspirin is generally avoided.

prenatal_vitamin.name: Prenatal vitamin
prenatal_vitamin.note: Recommended throughout pregnancy for folic acid, iron and DHA.

antacids_tums.name: Antacids (Tums)
antacids_tums.note: Calcium-based antacids are commonly used for heartburn.

diphenhydramine.name: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
diphenhydramine.note: Often considered okay short-term, but check with your provider.

ibuprofen_gel.name: Ibuprofen gel
ibuprofen_gel.note: Discuss topical NSAIDs with your provider before use.

isotretinoin.name: Isotretinoin (Accutane)
isotretinoin.note: Retinoids cause serious birth defects and must be avoided.

pseudoephedrine.name: Decongestant (pseudoephedrine)
pseudoephedrine.note: Generally avoided in the first trimester; ask your provider.

vitamin_a_high_dose.name: Vitamin A (high dose)
vitamin_a_high_dose.note: High-dose vitamin A can harm the baby; stick to prenatal amounts.

structure.beginner5k: Weeks 1 to 4 alternate short runs with walks, starting at 1 minute of running and building to 5-minute runs. Weeks 5 and 6 mix run and walk intervals with one continuous run. Weeks 7 to 9 are continuous runs of 25, 28 and then 30 minutes.
structure.fiveToTenK: Each week has two steady runs and a long run. The long run grows from 40 to 65 minutes. Every fourth week is lighter so you can recover, and the last week eases off.
structure.zone2Base: Each week has a short run, a middle run and a long run, all easy and held to Zone 2. Time in zone grows from 100 to 155 minutes a week, the long run from 40 to 70 minutes, and weeks 4 and 8 are lighter. Weeks 6, 7 and 9 end the short run with four relaxed strides. The middle run of weeks 4, 8 and 10 is a zone check.
structure.zone2Base4: Each week has two short runs, a middle run and a long run, all easy and held to Zone 2. Time in zone grows from 130 to 190 minutes a week, the long run from 40 to 70 minutes, and weeks 4 and 8 are lighter. Weeks 6, 7 and 9 end the first run with four relaxed strides. The middle run of weeks 4, 8 and 10 is a zone check.
structure.faster5k: Each week has a speed session (fast and easy repeats), an easy run and a longer run. In weeks 1 to 3 the longer run is easy; in weeks 4 to 6 it becomes a tempo run of 15, 20 and then 25 minutes.
structure.walkFit: Weeks 1 to 4 alternate stretches of brisk walking (3 to 8 minutes) with 2 minutes of easy walking. Weeks 5 and 6 use two longer brisk stretches of 12 and 15 minutes. Weeks 7 and 8 are continuous brisk walks of 20 to 30 minutes.
structure.halfMarathon: Each week has an easy run, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 50 to 115 minutes, every fourth week is lighter, and the last week is short before race day.
structure.marathon: Most weeks have two easy runs, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 70 minutes to 2¾ hours, every fourth week is lighter, and the last two weeks taper before race day.
structure.halfMarathon4: Each week has two easy runs, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 50 to 115 minutes, every fourth week is lighter, and the last two weeks taper before race day. The final week has three shorter runs.
structure.tenKToHalf4: Each week has two short runs, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 65 to 115 minutes, weeks 4 and 8 are lighter, and the last two weeks taper before race day. The final week has three shorter runs.
structure.fasterHalf4: Each week has a speed session, two easy runs and a long run. The long run builds from 70 to 110 minutes. Tempo runs of 25 and 30 minutes replace the speed session in weeks 6 and 8, week 4 is lighter, and the last three weeks taper before race day. The final week has three shorter runs.
structure.beginnerMarathon4: Each week has two short runs, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 70 minutes to 2½ hours, every fourth week is lighter, and the last three weeks taper before race day. The final week has three shorter runs.
structure.walk10k: Each week has two walks of brisk stretches with short easy breaks and one long brisk walk. The long walk grows from 40 to 105 minutes, weeks 4 and 8 are lighter, and the last week ends with the 10K walk.
structure.returnToRunning: Weeks 1 to 3 alternate short runs with walks, from 1-minute runs to 5-minute runs. Week 4 has three run/walk sessions with runs of 6, 10 and 12 minutes, adding up to 18, 20 and 22 minutes of running.
structure.gentle5k: Every week repeats one run/walk session three times. The runs grow from 30 seconds to 5 minutes by week 8, then to two 10-minute runs, a 15 and a 10-minute run, and finally continuous runs of 25 and 30 minutes.
structure.beginner10k: Weeks 1 to 6 follow the beginner 5K build from short runs and walks to continuous running. Weeks 7 to 12 are three runs a week. The long run grows from 30 to 60 minutes, and week 10 is lighter.
structure.faster10k: Each week has a speed session (fast repeats or hills), an easy run and a longer run. Week 4 is lighter. In weeks 5 to 7 the longer run is a tempo run of 20, 25 and then 30 minutes, and the last week eases off.
structure.tenKToHalf: Each week has a short run, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 65 to 115 minutes, weeks 4 and 8 are lighter, and the last two weeks taper before race day.
structure.fasterHalf: Each week has a speed session, an easy run and a long run. The long run builds from 70 to 110 minutes, tempo runs of 25 and 30 minutes replace the speed session in weeks 6 and 8, and the last two weeks taper.
structure.beginnerMarathon: Each week has a short run, a middle run and a long run. The long run builds from 70 minutes to 2½ hours, every fourth week is lighter, and the last three weeks taper before race day.
structure.advancedMarathon: Most weeks have two easy runs, a speed, hill or tempo session, a middle run and a long run. Most easy runs from week 3 end with strides. From week 9 the long run includes a block at marathon pace, except in the lighter weeks. The long run builds from 90 minutes to three hours, every fourth week is lighter, and the last two weeks taper before race day.

rest.title: Rest days
rest.beginner: Do not train on back-to-back days. Three workouts a week with a rest day between them, for example Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, gives your legs time to adapt. On rest days walk, stretch or do something gentle.
rest.fiveToTenK: Keep a rest day between the two steady runs, and put the long run a day or two after a rest day. Rest or cross-train (cycling, swimming, an easy walk) on the other days.
rest.zone2Base: Keep a rest day between runs where you can, and put the long run a day or two after a rest day. Easy runs add up quickly, so if you feel flat, take the day off rather than running harder. Rest or cross-train on the other days.
rest.faster5k: Give the speed session and the longer run an easy day or a rest day on each side. Never do them back to back. Spend the free days resting or cross-training gently.
rest.returnToRunning: Leave a day or two between runs, for example Monday, Thursday and Saturday, and keep every run easy and conversational. Rest, walk or cycle gently on the other days. If anything hurts more as you go, drop back to the previous week.
rest.fourRun: With four runs a week, take at least one full rest day and never run more than two days in a row. Keep the day before the long run easy or free, and rest or cross-train the day after it. Use the other days for rest, walking or low-impact cross-training.
rest.advanced: With five runs a week, take two rest or cross-training days and avoid more than two runs in a row. Keep the speed or tempo session and the long run at least two days apart, keep the days either side of them easy, and rest more in the lighter weeks.
rest.longDistance: Keep the day before the long run easy or free, and take a rest day the day after it. Space the other runs so no two hard days sit together, and use spare days for rest, walking or low-impact cross-training.

workout.title: Each workout
workout.body: A workout starts with a warm-up walk (a gentle jog before speed sessions), then its steps in order, then a cool-down walk. The app tells you when to switch, so you can put your phone away. Weeks are not tied to the calendar: if you miss a workout, the same one stays due.

run.title: How hard to run
run.body: Go by effort, not pace. Run slowly enough that you could talk in short sentences. If you cannot, slow down or take a walk break early. Beginner runs should feel easy to moderate, around 4 to 5 out of 10. Easy runs stay conversational, tempo runs feel comfortably hard (about 6 to 7 out of 10), and the fast pieces in speed sessions feel hard but controlled (7 to 8 out of 10), with the easy pieces between them a relaxed jog.

walk.title: How fast to walk
walk.body: Walk briskly but comfortably, about 5 to 6 km/h (3 to 3.5 mph), which is roughly 10 to 12 minutes per kilometer or 16 to 19 minutes per mile. Keep moving rather than stopping: the walks are for getting your breath back, so you should be able to talk normally by the end of each one. The warm-up and cool-down walks can be a little easier.

listen.title: Listening to your body
listen.body: Aches that settle after a day are normal; sharp or lasting pain is not, so stop and rest. If a week was too hard, repeat it or ask Sparky to ease the next workouts. Leave a rest day between workouts while you are starting out. This is general guidance, not medical advice: if you are unsure about starting a new exercise plan, check with your doctor first.

zone2.title: Zone 2 runs
zone2.body: Zone 2 is easy aerobic running: about 60 to 70 percent of your maximum heart rate. Zone 2 runs are held to a heart rate range, not a pace, because the same pace is harder on a hot day or a tired week. The Record screen shows the range and tells you when you are above or below it. If you have no heart rate reading, use the talk test: you should be able to speak in full sentences. Heart rate drifts up a little on a long run, so the top of the range loosens after 20 minutes. If your breathing is easy, a few beats over is fine; if it feels harder, slow down or walk. The range comes from your own heart rate zone settings; if you have not set a maximum, it is an estimate from your age, which can be off by ten beats or more either way. If it feels too easy or too hard, trust the talk test.
zone2.check: Weeks 4, 8 and 10 each have a zone check: the middle run. Run it on the same flat, familiar route at the same heart rate or effort, and compare your pace with the last one. If it is faster at the same effort, your base is growing. If you are slower, do not push: sleep, heat and stress show up here.

efforts.title: Strides, hills, tempo and marathon pace
efforts.body: A stride is a short, quick, relaxed effort of about 20 seconds, followed by a walk or jog back, done at the end of an easy run to loosen up. Hill repeats are hard efforts uphill with an easy walk or jog back down; pace does not matter on a hill, so judge them by effort. A tempo run is a steady stretch you could hold for about an hour, comfortably hard. Marathon pace is the pace you plan to hold on race day: practise it in the second half of long runs.

pace.title: Pace ranges
pace.body: Enter a recent race time under Your race pace and the Record screen can suggest a pace range for each kind of stretch. They are estimates: heat, hills or a tired week will change them, so use them as a guide and go by effort when the two disagree.
